owner.occupation: Textile artist and natural dyer, co-runs a cochineal cooperative link in Oaxaca

world.bio: I weave and dye in a studio in Coyoacán, Mexico City, and spend a week each month with nopal growers in Oaxaca whose cochineal I help sell. I write a small newsletter on natural dyes. I have written that farmed Peruvian cochineal mordanted with alum alone goes purple, and Oaxacan wild-harvest grana with a tin-and-cream-of-tartar mordant gives a true scarlet.
skills_assets: A dye studio in Coyoacán with eight vats and a loom room
A monthly week with nopal growers in the Oaxaca valley, direct contact with a cochineal cooperative
Technical knowledge of mordants: alum, tin, iron, cream of tartar, and their effects on cochineal
A newsletter with 2,400 subscribers, mostly textile artists and small brands
A small collection of reference swatches from over twelve years of dye tests

projects.name: Cochineal cooperative sales
projects.text: The cooperative in Oaxaca has 40 kg of dried cochineal from this season's harvest without a buyer at a fair price. Local middlemen offer 40 per cent below what the growers need. I have been posting samples to dye makers and textile brands abroad, but shipping and customs are slow, and most buyers want small lots.

projects.name: Grant report
projects.text: I owe a final report to a cultural foundation for a dye workshop I ran in May. The report is twelve pages and I have written three. The deadline passed two weeks ago and the programme officer has emailed twice.

notes.text: Back from Oaxaca on the night bus. The growers showed me this year's harvest, silver-grey cochineal on the nopal pads, the best I have seen in three years. The women are drying it on mats in the sun. They asked who will buy it. I said I am working on it.

Test batch: Peruvian farmed cochineal, alum only. It goes a cold purple, nothing like the scarlet people want. Oaxacan grana with tin and cream of tartar gives the red that looks like a pomegranate. I photographed both. Will post them in the newsletter.
Taught my son Mateo to drive in the empty car park at Perisur. He stalled four times and cried once. I said I stalled eleven times. It is not true. I stalled maybe six.

Studio roof leak again. The rains have not even peaked. Plumber says it needs waterproofing, 28,000 pesos. I can do it after the cooperative pays me my commission, but I cannot know when that will be.
Visited the market at Mercado de Artesanías. A woman sold me a hand-spun cotton skein at a fair price. We spoke about how to keep cochineal reds from fading. She said use less sun.
The foundation emailed again. I replied that I need another week. Opened the report and closed it. It has been two weeks.
Wrote half of the newsletter about why cheap alum-only cochineal goes purple. Three subscribers have replied already asking where to buy Oaxacan grana. I told them I would let them know.
40 kilos of cochineal sitting in the cooperative's storeroom, in a plastic bucket. If the humidity rises, it could spoil. I need to make a decision before the end of the month.

messages.text:
Don Eusebio: Lucía, the buyers from Puebla offered 1,200 pesos a kilo.
Me: That is far too low.
Don Eusebio: We need cash before the rains.
Me: Give me two weeks.

Mateo: Mama, can we drive again on Sunday?
Me: Yes, but you must not cry.
Mateo: I didn't cry.
Me: You did.

Officer: The report is due. Can you send it this week?
Me: I'll send it by Friday.
Officer: Thank you.
Me: I'm sorry for the delay.

Friend: I saw your newsletter. Do you ship small lots?
Me: Yes, 500 grams minimum.
Friend: I may have a buyer.
Me: Please send details.

relations.about: Lead of the Oaxaca cochineal cooperative, sixty-eight, counts on her for fair prices
Runs a small shop that buys natural dyes

constraints: Only sells ethically sourced cochineal, no wild-harvest from protected areas
Needs a buyer before the end of October
sensitive: The cooperative's finances depend partly on her sales
Overdue grant report is making her anxious
Roof repair money is tied to the cooperative's payment
